questions.question: What does a spanning list guarantee about every vector in $V$?
options: Every vector in $V$ has a unique length.
Every vector in $V$ is a linear combination of the list.
Every vector in $V$ is orthogonal to the list.
Every vector in $V$ is one of the listed vectors.

questions.question: Does $((1,0),(0,1),(1,1))$ span $\mathbb{R}^2$?
options: No, because three vectors cannot span a two-dimensional space.
No, because a spanning list cannot contain redundant vectors.
Yes, but only if $(1,1)$ is removed.
Yes, because the first two vectors already span $\mathbb{R}^2$.

questions.question: Does the list $((0,0))$ span $\mathbb{R}^2$?
options: Yes, because every spanning list must contain zero.
No, because zero vectors cannot be in any span.
No, its span is only $\{(0,0)\}$.
Yes, because it contains the zero vector.

questions.question: What is the difference between a spanning list and a basis?
options: A spanning list is shorter than a basis, because a basis also has to be independent.
A basis does not have to span the space.
A basis spans and is linearly independent; a spanning list may be redundant.
A spanning list cannot contain nonzero vectors.

questions.question: If a vector is removed from a spanning list, what can happen?
options: The remaining list may or may not span, depending on the removed vector's redundancy.
The vector space stops being finite-dimensional, since one spanning vector is missing.
The remaining list can never span.
The remaining list must always span.

questions.question: Does $((1,0,0),(0,1,0))$ span $\mathbb{R}^3$?
options: Yes, because the two vectors are linearly independent.
No, vectors with nonzero third coordinate cannot be generated.
No, because a spanning list of $\mathbb{R}^3$ must have exactly three vectors.
Yes, since $(0,0,1)$ is obtained by multiplying the two vectors.

questions.question: A spanning list of $V$ is a finite list $(\boldsymbol{v}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{v}_k)$ with $V=\operatorname{span}(\boldsymbol{v}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{v}_k)$. What does the word “finite” restrict?
options: The number of vectors in the list
The number of vectors in the space $V$
The number of scalars in the field
The number of ways to write a vector as a combination

questions.question: Which argument proves that a list of vectors in $\mathbb{R}^2$ spans $\mathbb{R}^2$?
options: Every $(a,b)\in\mathbb{R}^2$ is shown to be a combination of the list
The list is shown to have at least two vectors, all nonzero
The vector $(1,1)$ is shown to be a combination of the list
No vector of the list is shown to be a combination of the others

questions.question: How many ways are there to write $(3,4)$ as $a(1,0)+b(0,1)+c(1,1)$ with real $a,b,c$?
options: Infinitely many
Exactly one, since the list spans $\mathbb{R}^2$
Exactly two, with $c=0$ or $c=1$
None, since the list is redundant
